The AFCS features a Collective Safety Function that constantly monitors
engine power levels/MGB TQ and helicopter height above ground. This func -
tion is automatically activated whenever a collective upper mode is engaged
— AFCS Power Limiting: This limits the AFCS collective pitch demand dur -
ing high power phases of flight to prevent both MGB and engine limits
from being exceeded. When the AFCS power limiting is active, the amber
caption PWR LIM is displayed on the PFD (see Page 3-213 ). The function
activates to limit the maximum PI value in accordance with the following:
AEO conditions with IAS less than 90 KIAS: PI maximum 113%
AEO conditions with IAS greater than 90 KIAS: PI maximum 96%
— AFCS Autorotation protection: This limits the minimum collective pitch
demanded by the AFCS during steep descents to prevent entry into autor -
otation. The function activates when the engine TQ drops below 15%.
— AFCS LOW HEIGHT: This function prevents inadvertent helicopter
descent below the following radar height thresholds:

A tail rotor drive failure will result in a rapid yaw to the right and a loss of yaw
control, possibly accompanied by noise or vibration in the tail section. The
severity of the initial yaw rate will be determined by the airspeed, altitude,
gross weight, center of gravity and torque settings at the time that the failure
occurs. The effectiveness of the vertical fin in limiting the yaw rate and yaw
angle will depend on the airspeed at the time of the failure, fin effectiveness
The following cues will be present:
— Aircraft yaws rapidly to the right
— Loss of yaw control, pedals free but ineffective
— Possible noise and vibration from the aft fuselage area
Severe yaw rates will result in large yaw angles within a very short period of
time and, depending on the flight conditions at the time of failure, it is possible
that yaw angles in excess of 30° will be experienced.
Additionally, very high yaw rates will produce aircraft pitching and rolling mak -
ing retention of control difficult without the use of large cyclic inputs, which are
structurally undesirable. Finally, very high yaw rates will produce disorienting
effects on the pilots. Therefore, it is vital that corrective action, as outlined in
the following procedures, be taken quickly to prevent post-failure yaw rates
— Lower collective to LAND IMMEDIATELY while maintaining attitude
and minimizing lateral translation with the cyclic control.

and system operations are controlled by the control box and selection is by the

The Offshore/Elevated Helideck Take-Off technique (refer to in this supple -
ment as Offshore Helideck) considers the Pilot Flying (PF) and Pilot Not Flying
(PNF) coordinate their activities so that the PNF will monitor the height and
call out Take Off Decision Point (TDP) and, in the case of engine failure, the
rotor speed (NR) allowing the PF to concentrate on flying the manoeuvres.
The technique uses a vertical climb at 400 to 500 fpm (using up to 20% Delta
PI) above the helideck to achieve a TDP height of 25 ft (7.5 m) where a nose
down rotation commences for the flyaway . An engine failure before TDP
means the vertical climb must be stopped and the aircraft rejected back to the
helideck (RTO). An engine failure at or after the TDP means the pilot must
continue the rotation for a Continued Take Off (CTO) on one engine (OEI).
This Take-Off procedure also assures a deck edge clearance (always exceed -
ing 15 ft (5 m) vertical and 35 ft horizontal), even when the manoeuvre
requires a drop down Below the Take Off Surface (BTS).
The Take-Off manoeuvre is commenced with the helicopter nose wheel
approximately 2 m from the edge of the helideck.
When operating at the condition given in the Weight, Altitude, Temperature
(WAT) chart below, the technique above always assures no exposure time to a
ditching in case of an engine failure.
If the Take-Off WAT weight is such that in case of an engine failure a drop
down is required it is assumed that the height of the Elevated Helideck is
greater than the Drop Down plus a height clearance margin, as required by

The Rockwell Collins onboard Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System
(TCAS II) monitors a radius of nominal 14 NM around the helicopter by interro -
gating any intruding aircraft transponder and determining if a potential conflict
The system comprises of a TCAS II processor installed in the aft avionic bay
and two directional antennas one mounted on the top surface within the nose
radome and the second rear antenna is mounted under the rear part of the air -
The TCAS II system interrogates ICAO compliant transponders of aircraft in
the vicinity and based on replies received computes the relative range, altitude
(if included in the reply message), bearing and closure rate of other transpon -
der equipped aircraft with respect to the helicopter. The TCAS II calculates the
time to reach the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) with the intruder, this time
value is the main parameter for issuing alerts. If the transponder replies from
nearby aircraft includes their altitude, the TCAS II computes the time to reach
TCAS II issues two types of alerts:
— TAs (Traffic Advisory) to assist the visual search for the intruder aircraft
and prepare the pilot for a potential RA,
— RAs (Resolution Advisory) to define manoeuvres that will either increase
or maintain the existing vertical separation from the intruder aircraft.
When the intruder aircraft is also fitted with TCAS II, both TCAS II sys -
tems coordinate their RAs through the Mode S data link to ensure that

The Extended Range configuration consist of a modified lower fuselage sec -
tion with a modified fuel system, see Figure S22-2 . The modified lower section
incorporates three under floor fuel cells which are in addition to the to 2 main
fuel tanks (left hand and right hand). The three additional tanks are connected
together by a connecting tube allowing fuel to flow between the three tanks
and connected to the main tanks so refueling is carried out for all the tanks
from one gravity or pressure refueling point.
Fuel from the three underfloor tanks is transferred into the 2 main tanks by six
ejector pumps (three for each side). These ejector pumps are powered by the
main cells boost pumps assembly which contains two pumps per assembly.
Three ejectors for the right hand main cell and three for the left hand main cell.
The Fuel Gauging System automatically compensates for the additional fuel
quantity using additional dedicated fuel probes in the lower fuselage cells.
Power Plant Synoptic page fuel indication messages that may illuminate for
the Extended Range configuration are shown in Figure S22-1 .

The Circular Force Active Vibration Control System (CF AVCS) is designed to
reduce the 5R vibration levels experienced in the cockpit and cabin. The sys -
tem comprises of Circular Force Generator units mounted under the cabin and
cockpit floor, accelerometers mounted at a series of key positions on the fuse -
lage, rotor speed signal, an electronic integrated central controller unit (CC)
and a control panel, mounted in the interseat panel. The exact configuration
depends on the aircraft configuration and customer requirements.
The system takes signals from the vibration accelerometers and rotor speed
which are processed by the CC. Correction signals are then sent to the Circu -
lar Force Generators to minimise the vibrations.
The control panel Figure S29-1 consists of an OFF/ON switch with power indi -
cator, a built in TEST pushbutton, a system messages FAIL and a mainte -
nance port (MTN PORT) to connect maintenance and trouble shooting

The Obstacle Proximity LiDAR System (OPLS) presents to the pilot a visual
and audio indication of obstacle distances around the aircraft while in hovering
The system comprises of three Laser Imaging Detection and Ranging Units
(LiDAR) mounted around the aircraft transmission cowling below the rotor
head, a processing unit and audio/video adapters mounted in the rear avion -
ics bay, a control panel mounted in the interseat console (see Figure S30-2 )
and all necessary hardware and cabling (see Figure S30-1 ).
The LiDAR units generate digital distance profiles of the surrounding environ -
ment using a low-power, eye safe laser beam and receiver. The distance infor -
mation from the three overlapping beams are digitally mixed in the processors
to produce a 360° obstacle coverage, in the plane of the sensor units, around
the helicopter, see Figure S30-3 for sensor footprint (Note: no obstacles above
or below the plane or the sensor units is detected).
The information from the processor can then be displayed on the MFD using a
helicopter plan view representation with the obstacle profile on a polar grid
with range captions. The critical (minimum) distance to the nearest obstacle is
indicated by a colour coded radial line and the distance given at the top of the
display. Three colour bands are used for indicating criticality, Green (safe),
Yellow (caution) and Red (critical), see Figure S30-4 . In addition to the colour
coded indication an audio tone is also heard in the intercom which increases
in frequency as the distance decreases. An audio annunciation is heard pass -
ing from Green to Yellow “APPROACHING” and from Yellow to Red “CHECK
The OPLS Controller (Figure S30-2) is used to switch the system ON and OFF
and gives an indication of system status OFF/STBY/ON/ERROR.

The Automatic Foldable Step P/N 8G5260F00211 is an installation of 2 auto -

installed to illuminate the step at night.

the aircraft is on the ground, this selection can also be use. When selected
manually to be retracted a white status message “STEP RETRACTED” illumi -
nates on the CAS. If the step has not been retracted manually but remains
retracted whilst on the ground the white status message illuminates.

The maximum OEI engine ratings specified in Basic RFM Section 1 cannot be
used unless an actual engine failure occurs. Therefore, to permit pilot training
an Engine Training Mode enables OEI Training to be to carried out using a
reduced simulated OEI power which, combined with a reduced WAT weight,
permits realistic engine failure training manoeuvres.
The OEI Training function (OEI TRNG) is intended for Category A and 
Category B engine failure manoeuvre training.
The Training Mode system also provides safety devices in the event of an
incorrect training manoeuvre or an actual failure of the engine during training.
As the weight for the training manoeuvre is reduced, due to the reduced simu -
lated OEI power, then an incorrect training manoeuvre causing the training
mode to disengage restores full engine power to exit the condition.
The reduced engine power required for these manoeuvres also conserves
This Supplement details the limitations in WAT weight and usage of the
Engine Training Mode to carry out Category B operations and Category A T-O
The engine training mode incorporated in the engine EEC simulates an engine
failure and the corresponding single engine response and rotor speed charac -
teristics that are found in an actual engine failure.
To allow the trainee pilot to gain confidence, it is suggested that
before the maximum Training Weight is flown, a weight margin
is flown during the technique familiarization/build-up flights (e.g.
a weight reduction of, say, 200 kg). 

LIMITED ICING CLEARANCE AND ICING GENERAL
The Limited Ice Protection System (LIPS) permits flight into icing within a lim -
ited envelope of icing conditions without blade de-icing provided that the oper -
ational capability to descend into non-icing conditions is available throughout
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
the intended route. The ability to escape from icing conditions is required
because of the possibility of encountering ambient conditions more severe
than those permitted for continuos operation. For this purpose, the LIPS Limi -
tations include a requirement for at least a 500 ft band of positive temperature
air always to be available for the route being flown.
Continuous operation is possible within a defined severity of ambient icing
conditions and time limited operation is permitted in defined conditions of
greater severity. The purpose of the time limited area is to allow the crew to
take action to reduce the severity of the conditions being encountered, usually
by descending to allow natural de-icing of the aircraft. The crew are provided
with methods to monitor the icing severity and the effect on the aircraft.
The severity of the ice in icing conditions depends on the temperature and liq -
uid water content (LWC) and MVD. Different types of ice will form on the air -
craft depending on the icing conditions. The main types of ice are Glaze and
Rime. Glaze ice is clear and will tend to form at higher sub-zero temperatures
(0°C to -5°C) and is more likely with higher LWC and larger droplets. This type
of ice can generate high drag increase to occur due to the shape that forms.
Rime ice is white and opaque and tends to form at lower temperatures with
smaller droplets. Rime ice forms in a more streamlined shape and causes a
smaller increase in aircraft drag. It is possible to have a mixture of both, which
is known as Glime or Mixed Ice.
The PI variation, due to ice, can be expected to go possibly as high as 10%,
depending on OAT, LWC, and Water Droplet size (Mean Volumetric Diameter -
MVD). Higher PI increase may be experienced in more severe icing conditions
(higher LWC, larger MVD), but such conditions do not occur frequently in the
atmosphere. Cloud formations that are know to contain high levels of icing,
such as large vertical clouds, should be avoided.
Ice shedding from the MR will be experienced and this can be associated with
vibrations or seen and heard, with small pieces of ice striking the windscreens.
Flight in Freezing Rain or Freezing Drizzle is not permitted as it is not covered
by the current Airworthiness Rules for any type of aircraft. Freezing Rain and
Drizzle (also known as Supercooled Large Droplets - SLD) consists of super -
cooled water droplets of sizes greater than the EASA/FAA Part 29 
Appendix C, atmospheric definition used for Certification. These conditions,
although rare, have a serious effect on any aircraft’s performance.
Pilots must use normal operational planning and techniques to avoid flight in
these conditions. If encountered inadvertently, the conditions must be vacated
The LIPS system comprises of the following equipment:
— Ice severity meter and TIME IN ICE on the PFD ( Figure S48-2 )
— Heated windscreen system (powered by basic engine AC generators)
— Limited Ice Protection System control on ECDU ICE PROTECTION page.
— 2 Ice detectors and their associated processing units
— SLD Marker installed on the right side of the fuselage, in view of the pilot
The LIPS control box has two independent channels (A and B) which receive
the signals of OAT (from aircraft basic sensors via AMMS/ADS) and the two
ice detectors and determines the severity of the icing condition. The value of
the LWC, temperature and time have specific maximum limits which have
been determined for the ‘Limited Icing’ envelope. The exposure and severity
of the icing is indicated to the pilot by CAS cautions, advisory messages, an
Ice Severity Meter and “Time-In Ice” values on the PFD.
Icing is also indicated by a build up of ice on aircraft structure visible to the
pilot, e.g. unheated area of windscreens, wiper arms and SLD marker.
For any exceedance indicated by the system the action is to vacate the icing

With the LIPS selected OFF and a temperature below +4°C the CAS ICING
caution will illuminate, to indicate the system is OFF and icing conditions are
being approached. Selecting, on the ECDU ICE PROTECTION page, LIPS
ON the ICB, Ice Detectors and Windshield heating is automatically selected

Entry into the NO-LIMIT ZONE (Figure S48-2) causes the ICING caution to
illuminate for 5 seconds. The Ice Severity Meter indication will be in the green.
Entry into the “TIME-LIMITED ZONE” causes the ICE 5 MIN caution to illumi -
nate continuously and the Ice Severity Meter indication will be in the amber
section and “Time-In Ice” values display on the PFD.
The “Time in Ice” display counts down starting from 5 mins as the maximum
permitted time in this zone is 5 minutes. On expiry of the 5 minutes continuous
time or total cumulative time in this zone the ICE LIMIT caution illuminates
indicating to the pilot the icing conditions must be vacated. To clear the ICE
LIMIT caution a period of approximately 2 minutes in the “NO-ICE ZONE
(above 0°C) must be achieved, a period of 5 minutes in this zone is required to
reset the “TIME IN ICE counter to 5:00.
Entry into the “VACATE ZONE” causes the ICE LIMIT caution to illuminate
immediately and the Ice Severity Meter indication will be in the red indicating
to the pilot the icing conditions must be vacated. When the aircraft is back in
one of the reduced icing zones the caution extinguishes.
When vacating the icing zone if the aircraft enters “NO LIMIT ZONE” with the
Ice Severity indication in the green the “TIME IN ICING” count stops and
remains at the value when the zone was entered whether the entry into the
NO-LIMIT ZONE was due to expiry of the time limit or not. If the time limit has
not expired further excursions into the TIME LIMITED ZONE are permitted up
to the maximum time allowed (5 minutes).
If the “NO-ICE ZONE” conditions are entered the time remains at the value
when the zone was entered until a continuous time of 5 minutes has expired
(allowing the ice to shed) then the “TIME IN ICE” is removed from the display.
Also an SLD marker is installed on the right side of the fuselage above the
pilots head and visible through the upper screen. The SLD marker is a com -
posite sphere designed to help the pilot visually detect if SLD conditions are
encountered. The sphere has a black central circle with yellow and red rings
around it. Ice accretion can be easily seen on the black marker.

The IPS is designed to allow full icing operations by automatically de-icing MR
blades and anti-icing the TR blades.
Different types of ice will form on the aircraft depending on the icing condi -
tions. The main types of ice are Glaze and Rime. Glaze ice is clear and will
tend to form at higher sub-zero temperatures (0°C to -5°C) and is more likely
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
with higher LWC and larger droplets. This type of ice can generate high drag
increase to occur due to the shape that forms. Rime ice is white and opaque
and tends to form at lower temperatures with smaller droplets. Rime ice forms
in a more streamlined shape and causes a smaller increase in aircraft drag. It
is possible to have a mixture of both, which is know as Glime or Mixed Ice.
Flight in Freezing Rain or Freezing Drizzle is not permitted because it is not
covered by the current Airworthiness Rules for any type of aircraft. Freezing
Rain and Drizzle (also known as Supercooled Large Droplets - SLD) consists
of supercooled water droplets of sizes greater than the EASA/FAA CS/Part 29
Appendix C, atmospheric definition used for Certification. These conditions,
although rare, have a serious effect on any aircraft’s performance. Pilots must
use normal operational planning and techniques to avoid flight in these condi -
tions. If encountered inadvertently, the conditions must be vacated immedi -
The IPS system comprises of the following equipment:
— Heated windshield system (powered by the standard engine AC genera -
— Dedicated Main Gearbox mounted 30 KVA AC Generator, (the APU AC
generator providing emergency power when required)
— Heated Main and Tail Rotor blades with associated slip rings and wiring
— Ice severity meter on the PFD ( Figure S49-2 )
— IPS control pages within the ECDU
— 2 Ice detectors and their associated processing units
— SLD (Supercooled Liquid Droplet) Marker installed on the right side of the
fuselage, in view of the pilot through the upper screen.
Main rotor de-icing is provided by electrical heating of the main rotor blade
zones. There are six zones along the leading edge of the blade span; of these
6 zones the leading edge 3 are the critical zone and the aft 3 are the non-criti -
cal zone. These are heated sequentially. Tail rotor anti-icing is provided by
continuous heating of the leading edge of the blades.
Once selected ON via the ECDU the IPS is controlled automatically in relation
to the severity of the icing conditions encountered. The IPS is a dual channel
system that provides redundant ice protection for the main rotor blades. With
Channel A in control, heating of all of the main rotor zones, the pilot windshield
and the tail rotor are controlled, whilst Channel B remains as a dormant back-
up system for blade heating but controls the copilot windshield heating. In the
event of a failure of Channel A, after starting the APU, Channel B takes control
of the main rotor critical zones, (main rotor blade non-critical heating is lost)
and tail rotor blade heating, using the APU generator to power the ice protec -
tion system. The pilot windshield heating is lost.
In the event of a failure of Channel B there will be no blade heating system
redundancy remaining and the copilot windshield heating will be lost.
Electrical power for the heated blades is provided by a dedicated Main Gear -
box mounted AC generator. The power is controlled by the ICB and distributed
through distribution boxes and slip rings. Atmospheric information is provided
to the ICB by the Outside Air Temperature Sensors and the Ice Detectors. The
Ice Detectors and windshield heating are powered at all times with the IPS
ON; power is provided by the respective engine generator.
With the IPS selected ON and in AUTO mode on the ECDU (Figure S49-1), an
encounter with ice is indicated by the ICING caution illumination on the CAS,
when OAT is less than +4°C and a positive indication on the PFD Ice Severity
Meter ( Figure S49-2 ) . Icing is also indicated by a build-up of ice on visible air -
craft structure, e.g. unheated area of windshields, wiper arms, SLD marker.
In normal operation (AUTO mode) the main rotor de-icing system works by
allowing a small amount of ice to accrete on each leading edge zone and then
sequential heating of each zone removes the ice; the duration of these heating
cycles is variable depending on OAT and LWC. It is normal, therefore, to see

A failure of the primary IPS power supply will cause ‘IPS AC GEN FAIL’
caution to be generated and will cause complete loss of heating of both main
and tail rotors with associated ‘IPS MR FAIL’ warning and ‘IPS TR FAIL
caution. In this case the APU must be started immediately or the icing
conditions vacated. The APU Generator is used to supply power to the Tail
Rotor blades and the Critical Zones of the Main Rotor Blades. This will result
in the IPS MR DEGR caution to be displayed. Depending on the severity of
the icing conditions, torque and vibration can increase.
Note that in this case the Ice detectors, intake heaters and windshields will be
unaffected as these are supplied by the associated engine generators.
Failure of an engine generator will cause loss of the applicable windshield
heating and ice detector, which will generate ‘1(2) ICE DET FAIL’ and ‘1(2)
WSHLD HTR FAIL’ cautions and 1(2) INTAKE FAIL. In this case the
procedures for a Single Generator Failure should be followed.
The IPS Critical Zones are the three main rotor blade leading edge zones,
which are heated by dual power supplies and have duplicated control
systems. Failure of any of these zones causes the system to switch off,
resulting in a complete loss of main and tail rotor heating. The ‘IPS MR FAIL’
warning and ‘IPS TR FAIL’ caution will be generated.
In these cases, depending on the severity of the icing conditions, torque and
vibration can quickly increase resulting in the need to vacate icing conditions
MRB NON CRITICAL ZONE HEATING FAILURES
The IPS Non-Critical Zones are the three main rotor blade zones aft of the
leading edge critical zones. These zones are less likely to experience signifi -
cant ice accretions and their failure results in the ‘IPS MR DEGR’ caution to be
displayed. Depending on the severity of the icing conditions, torque and vibra -
The need to vacate icing conditions may be less urgent, but should be consid -
ered as the consequence of subsequent failures is more severe (loss of
redundancy). The non-critical zones have single power supply and single con -
trol systems. Tail rotor heating is not affected.
The Tail Rotor heating is connected in pairs of opposing blades so it is possi -
ble to have either pair of blades suffering a loss of heating, or all four blades
together. In the first case ‘IPS TR DEGR’ amber caution illuminates, while in
the second case the ‘IPS TR FAIL’ amber caution illuminates.
Loss of TR heating may result in a noticeable increase in TR vibration due to
asymmetric shedding of ice accumulations. After TR heating failure in icing,
the vibration can increase even after having exited icing conditions, due to the
natural shedding that occurs resulting in TR unbalance.
The IPS provides fully redundant de-icing control of the critical zones of the
MR blades. By default, the system control boxes’ channel A (ChA) and chan -
nel B (ChB) have assigned primary and back-up functions respectively.
A Channel A failure will result in the IPS MR FAIL warning to be generated
and will cause complete loss of heating of both main and tail rotors and pilot
windshield. In this case the APU must be started immediately or the icing con -
ditions vacated. The APU Generator is used to supply power to Channel B
resulting in the IPS MR DEGR caution being displayed. Depending on the
severity of the icing conditions, torque and vibration may increase.
If ARINC bus data from both ICB channels is lost the IPS DATA caution is
generated, resulting in the loss of valid IPS data (loss of ice severity indication
and system status) to the crew. In this case the icing conditions must be

Phenomena which may be experienced when flying in icing conditions are
This may occur after a double sensor failure, causing the IPS to function in
“default” mode. This uses default values to give a heating schedule which may
not be optimised for the atmospheric conditions and therefore may not com -
pletely de-ice the MR blades. This phenomenon may also occur with a MR
DEGR which could lead to ice accretion on the unheated MR non-critical
Runback Ice is formed by water running back from the leading edge of the
blade, past the heated zones and freezing. Because this ice forms behind the
heated zones the IPS cannot de-ice this area and the ice can have significant
effects on the aircraft including large torque rises and vibration.
This can be caused by selection of the system to OVRD mode or when the
default values give heating schedule higher than the ambient conditions
require. In either case the heating supplied is too high for the ambient condi -
tions. When the heating is too high, accreted ice is not broken and shed but
melted. The melt water travels backwards on the blade surface until it freezes
again on the cold (unheated) zones of the blade downstream, giving an
increase in drag and subsequent steady PI rise.
Both cases will give a steady increase in PI, sometime associated with asym -
metrical shedding and increase in vibrations. The pilot should be aware that,
in case of default mode functioning of IPS, he should closely monitor PI, OAT,
A/C vibrations and SLD marker, to understand the type of ice encountered.

MAIN ROTOR AND TAIL ROTOR SLIP RINGS
The Main Rotor Slip Ring transmits the power/signals between the MRLD,
which is fixed to the aircraft frame, and the MRUD, which rotates with the main
rotor blades. The Tail Rotor Slip Ring transmits the power/signals between the
TRD and TRLB, which are fixed to the aircraft frame, and the tail rotor heater
mats installed on the tail rotor blades.
Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
The Main Rotor Upper Distributor (MRUD) is a dual channel heater power dis -
tributor that controls the power delivered to the electro-thermal heating mats,
installed on the main rotor blades, as a function of the commands received by
— The MRLD through the main rotor slip ring
— The main rotor blades heater mats.
The Tail Rotor Distributor is a dual channel distributor that controls the power
to the tail rotor blades heater mats for the anti-icing function of the tail rotor
blades as requested by the ICB. The surface of the TR blades is maintained
within a fixed temperature band (from 35°C to 52°C) thus avoiding ice forma -
tion on them. Temperature control is obtained with 4 temperature sensors
(RTD), one installed inside each blade, used by TRD to manage the electrical
power supplied to the blades. The temperature values are inside the heater
mats and not on the blade surface. Heating is selected on when temperature
is below 35°C and selected off when temperature is above 52°C. Each chan -
nel of the TRD is connected to the two temperature sensors installed on the
adjacent tail rotor blades. The TRD reads only one temperature sensor for
each couple of opposite blades at a time, in the event of a failure of the first
sensor the TRD automatically switches to the opposite blades’ sensor to eval -
uate the temperature of the pair of blades.

The Limited Ice Protection System (LIPS) permits flight into icing within a lim -
ited envelope of icing conditions without blade de-icing provided that the oper -
ational capability to descend into non-icing conditions is available throughout

because of the possibility of encountering ambient conditions more severe
than those permitted for continuos operation. For this purpose, the LIPS Limi -

air always to be available for the route being flown.
Continuous operation is possible within a defined severity of ambient icing
conditions and time limited operation is permitted in defined conditions of
greater severity. The purpose of the time limited area is to allow the crew to
take action to reduce the severity of the conditions being encountered, usually
by descending to allow natural de-icing of the aircraft. The crew are provided
with methods to monitor the icing severity and the effect on the aircraft.
The severity of the ice in icing conditions depends on the temperature and liq -
uid water content (LWC) and MVD. Different types of ice will form on the air -
craft depending on the icing conditions. The main types of ice are Glaze and
Rime. Glaze ice is clear and will tend to form at higher sub-zero temperatures
(0°C to -5°C) and is more likely with higher LWC and larger droplets. This type
of ice can generate high drag increase to occur due to the shape that forms.
Rime ice is white and opaque and tends to form at lower temperatures with
smaller droplets. Rime ice forms in a more streamlined shape and causes a
smaller increase in aircraft drag. It is possible to have a mixture of both, which
is known as Glime or Mixed Ice.
The PI variation, due to ice, can be expected to go possibly as high as 10%,
depending on OAT, LWC, and Water Droplet size (Mean Volumetric Diameter -
MVD). Higher PI increase may be experienced in more severe icing conditions
(higher LWC, larger MVD), but such conditions do not occur frequently in the
atmosphere. Cloud formations that are know to contain high levels of icing,
such as large vertical clouds, should be avoided.
Ice shedding from the MR will be experienced and this can be associated with
vibrations or seen and heard, with small pieces of ice striking the windscreens.
Flight in Freezing Rain or Freezing Drizzle is not permitted as it is not covered
by the current Airworthiness Rules for any type of aircraft. Freezing Rain and
Drizzle (also known as Supercooled Large Droplets - SLD) consists of super -
cooled water droplets of sizes greater than the EASA/FAA Part 29 
Appendix C, atmospheric definition used for Certification. These conditions,
although rare, have a serious effect on any aircraft’s performance.
Pilots must use normal operational planning and techniques to avoid flight in
these conditions. If encountered inadvertently, the conditions must be vacated

Entry into the NO-LIMIT ZONE (Figure S50-2) causes the ICING caution to
illuminate for 5 seconds. The Ice Severity Meter indication will be in the green.
Entry into the “TIME-LIMITED ZONE” causes the ICE 5 MIN caution to illumi -
nate continuously and the Ice Severity Meter indication will be in the amber
section and “Time-In Ice” values display on the PFD.
The “Time in Ice” display counts down starting from 5 mins as the maximum
permitted time in this zone is 5 minutes. On expiry of the 5 minutes continuous
time or total cumulative time in this zone the ICE LIMIT caution illuminates
indicating to the pilot the icing conditions must be vacated. To clear the ICE
LIMIT caution a period of approximately 2 minutes in the “NO-ICE ZONE
(above 0°C) must be achieved, a period of 5 minutes in this zone is required to
reset the “TIME IN ICE counter to 5:00.
Entry into the “VACATE ZONE” causes the ICE LIMIT caution to illuminate
immediately and the Ice Severity Meter indication will be in the red indicating
to the pilot the icing conditions must be vacated. When the aircraft is back in
one of the reduced icing zones the caution extinguishes.
When vacating the icing zone if the aircraft enters “NO LIMIT ZONE” with the
Ice Severity indication in the green the “TIME IN ICING” count stops and
remains at the value when the zone was entered whether the entry into the
NO-LIMIT ZONE was due to expiry of the time limit or not. If the time limit has
not expired further excursions into the TIME LIMITED ZONE are permitted up
to the maximum time allowed (5 minutes).
If the “NO-ICE ZONE” conditions are entered the time remains at the value
when the zone was entered until a continuous time of 5 minutes has expired
(allowing the ice to shed) then the “TIME IN ICE” is removed from the display.

The Vernier Ice Accretion Meter is a twin bladed Vernier system illuminated to
allow use at night. The blades are engraved with sight lines and graduations to
permit the observer to determine the thickness of ice accreted on the airframe.

The windshields anti-icing is started as soon as the LIPS is switched ON,
not when LWC is detected. This is to give the crew the additional option
to de-mist the screens when the helicopter is out of the clouds.
The LIPS ICB has two independent, redundant channels (CH A & CH B) that
work in parallel. The ICB manages power to the two heated windshields, CH B
controls the pilot windshield (WSHLD 2) and CH A the copilot windshield
The operation of the windshield heating is automatic when the IPS is selected
ON. AC power from the engine AC generators supplies the windshield heating
elements and is regulated by values from the temperature sensors, fitted
within the windshields. These are used to turn the power on and off to main -
tain the temperature of the windshield between 35°C and 52°C. An overheat
threshold of 82°C is used by the ICB to shut down the relevant windshield
heating if the value is reached or superseded. If one or two of the three tem -
perature sensors fails the ICB uses the remaining sensors to control the
power. In the event of failure of all the three sensors the ICB indicates a

The ICB has two ARINC429 input lines (high speed) for the two ICE DETEC -
TOR signals. The ICB compares the LWC worst value (MAX) to the predefined
limits and signals and alarm if the limit has been exceeded. A failure of one ice
detector causes the ICB to use just the values from the other ice detector.
A further two ARINC429 lines (low speed) are used to receive the OAT values
from each AMMS (ADC 1 and 2), the system uses the lower of the two.

The Inlet Barrier Filter Kit (P/N 8G7160F00211) consists of an Engine Air Inlet
Barrier Filter P/N 8G7160F00611 and APU Air Inlet Barrier Filter P/N
8G4950F00111 which protects the engine and APU against ingestion of sand,
The system consists of two air inlet (2) filter assemblies, one mounted on each
engine cowling and an APU left/right and top air inlet filter assemblies ( Figure
The each filter assemby also contains a servo operated by-pass door which is
opened manually from the cockpit when the filters are blocked. The system is
controlled from the IBF page on the ECDU ( Figure S52-3 ), which permits the
manual opening of the the filter bypass doors.
The pressure drop across the intake filter is monitored by a pressure
transducer and when it reaches a predetermined value, due to the filters being
clogged with dust/dirt, then a ‘1(2) IBF PRESS’ or ‘APU IBF PRESS’ caution
illuminates on the CAS indicating that the engine or APU by-pass door must
be selected to OPEN. This is carried out from the ECDU IBF page selecting
the associated APU or ENG to OPEN. When open the 1(2) ENG IBF OPEN
or APU IBF OPEN advisory illuminates to indicate that the by-pass door is
open. When the by pass door is open the air entering the engine or APU is no
The filter assembly consists of a rigid aluminium frame with a media pack
constructed of pleated Synteq XP media (a dry media) with stainless steel
mesh screen on either side and provides filtered air to the engines or APU.
The media pack is sealed into the assembled frame.
When the Engine IBF is fitted engine intake heating does not function.

COMPARISON OF CAT A VERTICAL TYPE PROCEDURES
With the additional of the Confined Area procedure, found in this supplement,
the pilot may choose from the Ground/Elevated Heliport/Helideck Vertical
Procedure already presented in Supplement 4 Part A and the Confined
Procedure (provided the aircraft has the required Phase of software installed,
refer to General Limitation Section in this supplement) when obstacle
clearance may be required. Printed copy not contractually maintained by Leonardo Helicopters
Two different WAT charts, are available.
The general description of the Take-Off procedures follows:
• The Vertical Take-Off procedure comprises of a gentle vertical climb
above the take-off surface to a hover at the fixed TDP of 110 ft. The
pilot then initiates the transition forward and into the climb. At any time
during the vertical climb or at the hover point an engine failure dictates
a vertical OEI landing back to the take-off point. After the pilot has
committed to initiate the transition forward an engine failure will then
dictates a flyaway manoeuvre to be carried out. 
Refer to Supplement 4 Category A Operations .
• The Confined Area Take-Off procedure comprises on a rearward climb
from the centre of the ground level or elevated heliport. The climb is
carried out with a rearward groundspeed between 3 to 4 kt and a ROC
of between 300 fpm and 400 fpm. The climb angle is guaranteed
provided the heliport center point is maintained in sight between the
yaw pedals. This is maintained until the TDP is achieved which can be
varied between a minimum of 100 ft (30 m) ATS to a maximum of 200
ft (60 m) ATS (TDP ), depending on the obstacles in the take-off flight
path, altitude, temperature and aircraft weight. At any time during the
rearwards climb an engine failure up to and including TDP dictates an
OEI landing back to the take-off point which remains in sight
throughout the rejected procedure and touchdown.

The general description of the Landing procedures follows:
• The Helipad Vertical Landing procedure consists of a slow approach to
a high hover vertically above the landing surface with a fixed LDP at
110 ft proceeded by a slow descent to HIGE and landing. An engine
failure anywhere prior to the 110 ft hover LDP point requires a balked
landing to be carried out with a fixed Balked Landing profile.

• The Confined Area Landing technique comprises of a steep approach

pilot flying). The approach is started at a point 150 ft above the chosen
LDP with a descent of 200 fpm and 10 to 15 kt GS. Approaching the
LDP value chosen the nose is rotated to align the helipad between the
yaw pedals The speed is reduced to 4-6 kt groundspeed and 400 fpm
to 600 fpm ROD which results in a 45 degree glideslope. From the LDP
the descent approach is continued to a hover at the centre of the
The landing allows a variable LDP (LDP V ) between 200 ft to 100 ft ALS
to cater for possible obstacles in the Balked Landing profile.

The Confined Area Take-Off procedure comprises on a rearward climb from
the centre of the ground level or elevated heliport. The climb is carried out with
a rearward groundspeed between 3 to 4 kt and a ROC of between 300 fpm
and 400 fpm. The climb angle is guaranteed provided the heliport center point
is maintained in sight between the yaw pedals. This is maintained until the
TDP is achieved which can be varied between a minimum of 100 ft (30 m)
ATS to a maximum of 200 ft (60 m) ATS, depending on the obstacles in the
take-off flight path, altitude, temperature and aircraft weight. 

The Confined Area Landing technique comprises of a steep approach to the
helipad with an initial 20° yaw left (or to the right depending on pilot flying).
The approach is started at a point 150 ft above the chosen LDP with a descent
of 200 fpm and 10 to 15 kt Groundspeed. Approaching the LDP value chosen
the nose is rotated to align the helipad between the yaw pedals and the speed
reduced to 4-6 kt groundspeed and 400 fpm to 600 fpm ROD which produces
a 45 degree glideslope. From the LDP the descent approach is continued to
the hover at the centre of the helipad.

The bleed flow is limited by the size of the engine and APU bleed ducts

The duct temperature sensor monitors the mixed air temperature

The mixed air exiting the jet pump is delivered to the cockpit and cabin
through flexible and rigid ducts of similar construction to the ventilation
ducts. The heating air is routed down the rear fuselage cabin bulkhead
and forwards under the fuel tanks to the cabin where it divides into two
ducts running in parallel along the centre of the aircraft under the cabin
floor, one for the cockpit and one for the cabin.
The left (port) duct provides the cabin heating air, feeding fixed outlet
diffusers in the aft and forward corners of the cabin. The right (starboard)
duct provides the cockpit supply with the air being ducted forward along
the aircraft under the cabin floor before integrating with the cockpit
ventilation system in the cockpit centre console.

The fire detection system consists of a fire wire (Figure 7-39) containing a
fixed quantity of inert gas (helium) with an internal metal core filled with an
active gas and a pressure transducer. The metal core is capable of releasing a
large quantity of the active gas within the fire wire when a small section of its
surface reaches high temperature, this results in an increase of pressure and

The APU bay is equipped with an independent fire warning system. The

The baggage smoke detection system consists of a smoke detector
( Figure 7-40 ) installed on the roof of the baggage compartment. Four screws
and four washers attach the smoke detector to the related support socket.
The smoke detector is a photoelectric device that uses the Tyndall effect (light
scattering). When a beam of light goes through air that contains smoke, the
smoke particles cause the reflection of the incident light at an angle with the
axis of the light beam (light scattering). The intensity of the light scattering is
dependent on the concentration of the smoke.
The smoke detector uses an electronic circuitry to transmit pulses of light at
constant intervals and to measure the light scattering.

The two engines are housed in a compartment located aft of the transmission.
A front and rear firewall enclose the engine compartment and a central firewall

The engines are equipped with drain tubes which protrude from the underside

The CT7-2E1 engine is a compact, lightweight gas turbine engine with a sea
level power output in the 2,100 horsepower range.
The engine incorporates a five stage axial/one stage centrifugal compressor,
an annular combustor, a two stage, air cooled, gas generator turbine and a
two stage un-cooled power turbine with a drive shaft extending forward

The compressor has one stage of variable inlet guide vanes and two stages of
variable stator vanes that, together with an engine mounted start bleed valve,
ensure efficient and surge free engine operation through the entire operating
range. An integral inlet particle separator protects the engine from foreign
object damage and the ingestion of sand and dust.

The purpose of the Circular Force Active Vibration Control System (identified
as CF AVCS) P/N 8G1830F00111 is to decrease the vibrations in the fuselage
that are caused by the main rotor and the main gearbox.
The CF AVCS measures the vibrations with its accelerometers installed under
the cockpit and the cabin structures. The accelerometers signals are supplied
to the AVCS central controller. The AVCS central controller processes the
accelerometers signals and generates the command signals for the circular
force generators. The circular force generators supply the dynamic forces that
are necessary to decrease the vibrations.

MAIN AND TAIL ROTOR TIE DOWN
Tie down main rotor whenever any of the following condition exist:
1. Thunderstorms are in the local area or forecasted.
2. Winds up to, but not exceeding, 50 knots.
3. Helicopter is parked within 150 ft of hovering or taxiing aircraft that are in
excess of 5400 kg (11,900 pounds) gross weight.
The main rotor tie downs are socks which fit over the end of each blade with
cords which attach to mooring points on the fuselage. The tie down cords are
manufactured to specified lengths for forward and aft mooring points, as
identified by streamers adjacent to the brass rings to which the snap hooks
attach. When secure, the tie downs should be free of slack or under slight
tension, but not under sufficient tension to flex the main rotor blades
appreciably. The cords should never be shortened from their design lengths,
as excessive loads could be induced in the main rotor yokes.
The tail rotor tie down is red and is stenciled in white letters “REMOVE
BEFORE FLIGHT”. To tie down the tail rotor assembly, rotate main rotor until
tail rotors are aligned with the vertical fin and main rotor blades are
approximately 45 degrees to helicopter centerline. Tie down main rotor first,
then secure tail rotor with tail rotor blades flapping block.
